claim: Poor air quality has been linked to cognitive deficits in children.
source: Poor air quality has been linked to cognitive deficits in children, but this relationship has not been examined in the first year of life when brain growth is at its peak.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: The relationship between poor air quality and cognitive deficits has not been examined in the first year of life when brain growth is at its peak.
source: Poor air quality has been linked to cognitive deficits in children, but this relationship has not been examined in the first year of life when brain growth is at its peak.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in the literature, representing established knowledge about what has not been studied.

claim: In-home air quality focusing on particulate matter with diameter of <2.5 μm (PM2.5) and infants' cognition were measured longitudinally in a sample of families from rural India.
source: We measured in-home air quality focusing on particulate matter with diameter of <2.5 μm (PM2.5) and infants' cognition longitudinally in a sample of families from rural India.
evidence: This describes the methods used in the study.

claim: Air quality was poorer in homes that used solid cooking materials.
source: Air quality was poorer in homes that used solid cooking materials.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Infants from homes with poorer air quality showed lower visual working memory scores at 6 and 9 months of age.
source: Infants from homes with poorer air quality showed lower visual working memory scores at 6 and 9 months of age and slower visual processing speed from 6 to 21 months when controlling for family socio-economic status.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Infants from homes with poorer air quality showed slower visual processing speed from 6 to 21 months when controlling for family socio-economic status.
source: Infants from homes with poorer air quality showed lower visual working memory scores at 6 and 9 months of age and slower visual processing speed from 6 to 21 months when controlling for family socio-economic status.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Poor air quality is associated with impaired visual cognition in the first two years of life.
source: Thus, poor air quality is associated with impaired visual cognition in the first two years of life, consistent with animal studies of early brain development.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The association between poor air quality and impaired visual cognition in the first two years of life is consistent with animal studies of early brain development.
source: Thus, poor air quality is associated with impaired visual cognition in the first two years of life, consistent with animal studies of early brain development.
evidence: This connects the study's findings to prior animal research.

claim: This is the first demonstration of an association between air quality and cognition in the first year of life using direct measures of in-home air quality and looking-based measures of cognition.
source: We demonstrate for the first time an association between air quality and cognition in the first year of life using direct measures of in-home air quality and looking-based measures of cognition.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's approach and findings.

claim: Indoor air quality was linked to cooking materials in the home.
source: Because indoor air quality was linked to cooking materials in the home, our findings suggest that efforts to reduce cooking emissions should be a key target for intervention.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Efforts to reduce cooking emissions should be a key target for intervention.
source: Because indoor air quality was linked to cooking materials in the home, our findings suggest that efforts to reduce cooking emissions should be a key target for intervention.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: The Global Burden of Disease Study in India attributed 1.67 million deaths in 2019 to air pollution-related causes.
source: This impact was recently quantified by the Global Burden of Disease Study in India, attributing 1.67 million deaths in 2019 to air pollution-related causes with an overall national economic loss of $36.8 billion (Pandey et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pandey et al., 2021.

claim: Air pollution in India resulted in an overall national economic loss of $36.8 billion in 2019.
source: This impact was recently quantified by the Global Burden of Disease Study in India, attributing 1.67 million deaths in 2019 to air pollution-related causes with an overall national economic loss of $36.8 billion (Pandey et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pandey et al., 2021.

claim: Economic losses from poor air quality are compounded by evidence that poor air quality impacts neurocognitive health in childhood as economic losses accumulate over years of reduced productivity.
source: Such economic losses are compounded by evidence that poor air quality impacts neurocognitive health in childhood as economic losses accumulate over years of reduced productivity (Heckman and Mosso, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heckman and Mosso, 2014.

claim: Poor air quality and proximity to roadways is associated with reduced general cognitive functioning in childhood.
source: Studies have reported that poor air quality and proximity to roadways is associated with reduced general cognitive functioning in childhood (Freire et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009; Harris et al., 2015; Suglia et al., 2008) and slower growth in working memory (Sunyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Poor air quality and proximity to roadways is associated with slower growth in working memory in childhood.
source: Studies have reported that poor air quality and proximity to roadways is associated with reduced general cognitive functioning in childhood (Freire et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2009; Harris et al., 2015; Suglia et al., 2008) and slower growth in working memory (Sunyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sunyer et al., 2015.

claim: Exposure to poor air quality is a risk factor for child emotional and behavioural problems which can have severe impacts on families.
source: Exposure to poor air quality is also a risk factor for child emotional and behavioural problems which can have severe impacts on families (Midouhas et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Midouhas et al., 2019.

claim: Animal studies show profound impacts on the brain in early development from air pollution exposure.
source: This is an important question as animal studies show profound impacts on the brain in early development, with inhalation of diesel exhaust and ultrafine particles resulting in elevated cytokine expression and oxidative stress in the brain (Gerlofs-Nijland et al., 2010; Bos et al., 2012), as well as altered neurogenesis (Patten et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to animal studies.

claim: Inhalation of diesel exhaust and ultrafine particles results in elevated cytokine expression and oxidative stress in the brain.
source: This is an important question as animal studies show profound impacts on the brain in early development, with inhalation of diesel exhaust and ultrafine particles resulting in elevated cytokine expression and oxidative stress in the brain (Gerlofs-Nijland et al., 2010; Bos et al., 2012), as well as altered neurogenesis (Patten et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gerlofs-Nijland et al., 2010 and Bos et al., 2012.

claim: Inhalation of diesel exhaust and ultrafine particles results in altered neurogenesis.
source: This is an important question as animal studies show profound impacts on the brain in early development, with inhalation of diesel exhaust and ultrafine particles resulting in elevated cytokine expression and oxidative stress in the brain (Gerlofs-Nijland et al., 2010; Bos et al., 2012), as well as altered neurogenesis (Patten et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Patten et al., 2020.

claim: Very small particulate fragments (particulate matter with diameter of <2.5 μm; PM2.5) can move from the respiratory tract into the circulatory system reaching the brain.
source: Very small particulate fragments (particulate matter with diameter of <2.5 μm; PM2.5) are of major concern as they can move from the respiratory tract into the circulatory system reaching the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PM2.5.

claim: The brain may be particularly sensitive during infancy due to an immature detoxification response.
source: The brain may also be particularly sensitive during infancy due an immature detoxification response (Grandjean and Landrigan, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grandjean and Landrigan, 2014.

claim: Several large-scale studies have looked at the effects of prenatal exposure to nitrous oxide and PM2.5 on human cognition early in development.
source: Several large-scale studies have looked at the effects of prenatal exposure to nitrous oxide and PM2.5 on human cognition early in development (Guxens et al., 2012; Guxens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guxens et al., 2012 and 2014.

claim: Prenatal exposure to nitrous oxide and PM2.5 results in reduced psychomotor functioning at 1–6 years of age.
source: Results show reduced psychomotor functioning at 1–6 years of age, but no associations with early cognition, although three studies have reported slower cognitive growth and emotional / conduct problems in children exposed to poorer indoor air quality as assessed via questionnaires (Midouhas et al., 2019; Gonzalez-Casanova et al., 2018; Vrijheid et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the citations to studies on prenatal exposure.

claim: Prenatal exposure to nitrous oxide and PM2.5 shows no associations with early cognition.
source: Results show reduced psychomotor functioning at 1–6 years of age, but no associations with early cognition, although three studies have reported slower cognitive growth and emotional / conduct problems in children exposed to poorer indoor air quality as assessed via questionnaires (Midouhas et al., 2019; Gonzalez-Casanova et al., 2018; Vrijheid et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from prior studies.

claim: Three studies have reported slower cognitive growth and emotional/conduct problems in children exposed to poorer indoor air quality as assessed via questionnaires.
source: Results show reduced psychomotor functioning at 1–6 years of age, but no associations with early cognition, although three studies have reported slower cognitive growth and emotional / conduct problems in children exposed to poorer indoor air quality as assessed via questionnaires (Midouhas et al., 2019; Gonzalez-Casanova et al., 2018; Vrijheid et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Midouhas et al., 2019; Gonzalez-Casanova et al., 2018; Vrijheid et al., 2012.

claim: No studies have looked at the relationship between poor air quality and cognition in the first year of life when brain size doubles.
source: Critically, no studies have looked at the relationship between poor air quality and cognition in the first year of life when brain size doubles and may be particularly sensitive to toxins.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in the literature.

claim: Brain size doubles in the first year of life.
source: Critically, no studies have looked at the relationship between poor air quality and cognition in the first year of life when brain size doubles and may be particularly sensitive to toxins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about brain development.

claim: The brain may be particularly sensitive to toxins in the first year of life.
source: Critically, no studies have looked at the relationship between poor air quality and cognition in the first year of life when brain size doubles and may be particularly sensitive to toxins.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on knowledge of brain development.

claim: Standardized measures of infant cognition may not generalize to non-Western cultures where air quality is poorest.
source: While standardized measures exist (e.g. Mullen Scales of Early Learning), these tools may not generalize to non-Western cultures where air quality is poorest.
evidence: This is a concern raised about the generalizability of standardized measures.

claim: Multiple aspects of visual cognition that are predictive of later cognitive abilities can be measured reliably in the first year across cultures using looking-based tasks.
source: Multiple aspects of visual cognition that are predictive of later cognitive abilities (Rose et al., 2012) can be measured reliably in the first year across cultures (Rose, 1994; Wijeakumar et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rose et al., 2012; Rose, 1994; Wijeakumar et al., 2019.

claim: Visual processing speed measured using looking-based tasks in both infancy and toddlerhood is significantly predictive of working memory and executive function scores at 11 years.
source: For instance, visual processing speed measured using looking-based tasks in both infancy and toddlerhood is significantly predictive of working memory and executive function scores at 11 years (Rose et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rose et al., 2012.

claim: Infants spend much of the first year indoors.
source: A second challenge is that infants spend much of the first year indoors.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about infant behavior.

claim: Data from outdoor monitoring stations may not accurately reflect air quality exposure critical for early brain development, particularly in contexts where use of solid fuels in cooking may lead to differences between indoor and outdoor air quality.
source: Consequently, data from outdoor monitoring stations may not accurately reflect air quality exposure critical for early brain development, particularly in contexts where use of, for instance, solid fuels in cooking may lead to differences between indoor and outdoor air quality.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of outdoor air quality monitoring for assessing infant exposure.

claim: Recent advances in air quality monitoring allow for the measurement of PM2.5 directly in homes.
source: Recent advances in air quality monitoring allow for the measurement of PM2.5 directly in homes; this may be critical as PM2.5 is possibly the most neurotoxic component of residential air quality (Block and Calderón-Garcidueñas, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about technological advances.

claim: PM2.5 is possibly the most neurotoxic component of residential air quality.
source: Recent advances in air quality monitoring allow for the measurement of PM2.5 directly in homes; this may be critical as PM2.5 is possibly the most neurotoxic component of residential air quality (Block and Calderón-Garcidueñas, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Block and Calderón-Garcidueñas, 2009.

claim: The visual cognition task used in this study capitalizes on infants' tendency to look away from visual familiarity and toward visual novelty.
source: To assess visual cognition, we used a specially-designed, transculturally-relevant visual cognition task which assessed infants' visual working memory and processing speed (Figure 1A and B; see Ross-Sheehy et al., 2003), capitalizing on infants' tendency to look away from visual familiarity and toward visual novelty.
evidence: This describes the theoretical basis of the task design.

claim: The visual cognition task has been examined in several prior studies.
source: This task has been examined in several prior studies (Oakes et al., 2006; Oakes et al., 2009), but this is the first study to use this task longitudinally with a sample of non-western infants.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oakes et al., 2006 and 2009.

claim: This is the first study to use the visual cognition task longitudinally with a sample of non-western infants.
source: This task has been examined in several prior studies (Oakes et al., 2006; Oakes et al., 2009), but this is the first study to use this task longitudinally with a sample of non-western infants.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study design.

claim: If infants can remember the colors in working memory, they should lose interest in the 'no change' display and release fixation to visually explore the 'changing' display.
source: If infants begin looking at the 'no change' side and they can remember the colors in working memory, they should lose interest in this display, releasing fixation to visually explore the 'changing' display.
evidence: This describes the expected behavior based on the task design.

claim: When the number of items on the screen is small (i.e. the memory load is low), infants can detect the difference between the 'no change' and 'change' displays, and they show a higher change preference.
source: When the number of items on the screen is small (i.e. the memory load is low), infants can detect the difference between the 'no change' and 'change' displays, and they show a higher change preference.
evidence: This describes the expected behavior based on the task design.

claim: With increasing memory load (and increasing difficulty), infants may falsely detect changes on the 'no change side' and have difficulty releasing fixation, leading to a lower change preference.
source: With increasing memory load (and increasing difficulty), infants may falsely detect changes on the 'no change side' and have difficulty releasing fixation, leading to a lower change preference (Perone et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the expected behavior based on the task design, supported by a citation to Perone et al., 2011.

claim: The change preference score yields a quantifiable measure of infants' visual working memory abilities.
source: Thus, the change preference score yields a quantifiable measure of infants' visual working memory abilities.
evidence: This is a claim about what the task measures.

claim: The study was conducted in Shivgarh, India, a rural community in Uttar Pradesh.
source: Our study was conducted in Shivgarh, India, a rural community in Uttar Pradesh, one of the states in India that has been most strongly impacted by poor air quality (Pandey et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the study location.

claim: Uttar Pradesh is one of the states in India that has been most strongly impacted by poor air quality.
source: Our study was conducted in Shivgarh, India, a rural community in Uttar Pradesh, one of the states in India that has been most strongly impacted by poor air quality (Pandey et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pandey et al., 2021.

claim: Data were reported from 215 families from a range of socio-economic backgrounds.
source: We report data from 215 families from a range of socio-economic backgrounds (see Table 1).
evidence: This describes the study sample.

claim: Infants were enrolled at 6 months (N=108) or 9 months of age (N=107).
source: Infants were enrolled at 6 months (N=108) or 9 months of age (N=107) at which time they completed an in-lab assessment of visual cognition (see Figure 1A) as well as standardized psychomotor and cognitive assessments.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: A similar assessment was repeated a year later when the same infants were 18 or 21 months of age.
source: A similar assessment was repeated a year later when the same infants were 18 or 21 months of age (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the longitudinal study design.

claim: There is an improvement in visual working memory capacity between 6 and 8 months.
source: We examined these two cohorts based on evidence that there is an improvement in visual working memory capacity between 6 and 8 months.
evidence: This is stated as established evidence motivating the cohort selection.

claim: 6.5-month-old infants demonstrate greater-than-chance change preference scores with a memory load of one item.
source: In particular, Ross-Sheehy and colleagues (Ross-Sheehy et al., 2003) showed that 6.5-month-old infants demonstrate greater-than-chance change preference scores with a memory load of one item, while 10- and 13-month-old infants showed greater-than-chance change preference scores for memory loads of two and three items.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ross-Sheehy et al., 2003.

claim: 10- and 13-month-old infants showed greater-than-chance change preference scores for memory loads of two and three items.
source: In particular, Ross-Sheehy and colleagues (Ross-Sheehy et al., 2003) showed that 6.5-month-old infants demonstrate greater-than-chance change preference scores with a memory load of one item, while 10- and 13-month-old infants showed greater-than-chance change preference scores for memory loads of two and three items.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ross-Sheehy et al., 2003.

claim: 6.5-month-old infants could remember one spatial location.
source: Similarly, 6.5-month-old infants could remember one spatial location, while 8- and 12.5-month-old infants showed evidence of remembering multiple locations (Oakes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oakes et al., 2011.

claim: 8- and 12.5-month-old infants showed evidence of remembering multiple locations.
source: Similarly, 6.5-month-old infants could remember one spatial location, while 8- and 12.5-month-old infants showed evidence of remembering multiple locations (Oakes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oakes et al., 2011.

claim: 257 families were brought to the lab for the VWM and cognitive assessment.
source: We brought 257 families to the lab for the VWM and cognitive assessment; however, 17 families (10 6-month-old infants; 7 9-month-old infants) did not complete the assessment and were dropped from the study.
evidence: This describes the initial sample size.

claim: 17 families did not complete the assessment and were dropped from the study.
source: We brought 257 families to the lab for the VWM and cognitive assessment; however, 17 families (10 6-month-old infants; 7 9-month-old infants) did not complete the assessment and were dropped from the study.
evidence: This describes attrition in the study.

claim: 240 families were followed up for the duration of the study which spanned two years.
source: The remaining 240 families were followed up for the duration of the study which spanned two years and included the following: (1) a laboratory assessment in year 1 at 6 or 9 months of age; (2) a home visit every three months thereafter for the remainder of year 1 (e.g. at 9, 12, and 15 months of age for the 6 month cohort); (3) a laboratory assessment in year 2 at 18 or 21 months of age; (4) a home visit every three months thereafter for the remainder of year 2 (e.g. at 21, 24, and 27 months of age for the 6-month cohort).
evidence: This describes the longitudinal study design.

claim: Enrollment was distributed over 4 waves separated by 3 months, such that approximately 60 infants per wave were enrolled.
source: Enrollment was distributed over 4 waves separated by 3 months, such that we enrolled approximately 60 infants per wave of data collection (for a full list of data collected in the study, see Supplementary Materials).
evidence: This describes the enrollment strategy.

claim: The study was approved by the Community Empowerment Lab Institutional Ethics Committee (Ref. No: CEL/2018005).
source: The study was approved by the Community Empowerment Lab Institutional Ethics Committee (Ref. No: CEL/2018005).
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: Air quality data were collected for a total of 219 children.
source: Air quality data were collected for a total of 219 children; of those, 215 had data that survived initial data quality checks (described below).
evidence: This describes the air quality data collection.

claim: 215 children had air quality data that survived initial data quality checks.
source: Air quality data were collected for a total of 219 children; of those, 215 had data that survived initial data quality checks (described below).
evidence: This describes the final sample with usable air quality data.

claim: 213 children had data from the visual working memory task and cognitive assessment during either the first or second laboratory assessment.
source: 213 children also had data from the visual working memory task and cognitive assessment during either the first laboratory assessment (when infants were 6 or 9 months of age) or the second laboratory assessment (when infants were 18 or 21 months of age).
evidence: This describes the sample with cognitive data.

claim: 204 participants contributed visual working memory data in year 1.
source: In particular, 204 participants contributed visual working memory data in year 1 when they were 6 months of age (N=109; N girls = 50; M age = 182.4 days, SD age = 14.9 days) or 9 months of age (N=95; N girls = 51; M age = 267.2 days, SD age = 14.2 days).
evidence: This describes the year 1 sample.

claim: 181 participants contributed visual working memory data in year 2.
source: In year 2, 181 participants contributed visual working memory data when the infants were 18 months of age (N=90; N girls = 45; M age = 546.2 days, SD age = 19.2 days) or 21 months of age (N=91; N girls = 45; M age = 627.4 days, SD age = 27.7 days).
evidence: This describes the year 2 sample.

claim: Family SES data were obtained using the modified Kuppuswamy Scale.
source: As part of the first laboratory visit, caregivers were interviewed to obtain demographic indices and family SES data using the modified Kuppuswamy Scale (Mohd Saleem, 2020).
evidence: This describes the SES measurement method.

claim: The modified Kuppuswamy Scale classifies SES using occupation, education, and family income.
source: This scale classifies SES using occupation, education, and family income.
evidence: This describes the components of the SES scale.

claim: A 42-inch LCD monitor connected to a PC running Experiment Builder was used to display the stimuli.
source: A 42-inch LCD monitor that was connected to a PC running Experiment Builder was used to display the stimuli.
evidence: This describes the equipment used in the study.

claim: Looking data were collected at 500 Hz using an Eyelink 1000 Plus eye-tracker.
source: Looking data were collected at 500 Hz using an Eyelink 1000 Plus eye-tracker (SR Research).
evidence: This describes the data collection method.

claim: Where eye-tracking data were not available, looking data were collected with a webcam and hand-coded at 30 frames-per-second using Datavyu.
source: Where eye-tracking data were not available, looking data were collected with a webcam and hand-coded at 30 frames-per-second using Datavyu, 2014.
evidence: This describes an alternative data collection method.

claim: Infants sat on their mother's lap 100 cm from the screen.
source: Infants sat on their mother's lap 100 cm from the screen.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: The stimuli consisted of two side-by-side flickering displays composed of colored squares.
source: The stimuli consisted of two side-by-side flickering displays composed of colored squares (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the visual stimuli used in the task, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Standardized psychomotor and cognitive assessments were collected in year 1 using the Mullen Scales of Early Learning (MSEL).
source: We collected standardized psychomotor and cognitive assessments in year 1 using the Mullen Scales of Early Learning (MSEL).
evidence: This describes the standardized assessment used in year 1.

claim: In year 2, the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (3rd edition; ASQ) was used.
source: In year 2, we used the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (3rd edition; ASQ).
evidence: This describes the standardized assessment used in year 2.

claim: The switch to ASQ in year 2 was because preliminary testing with the MSEL revealed many questions that were not relevant to the rural setting in Shivgarh.
source: We switched to the ASQ in year 2 because preliminary testing with the MSEL revealed many questions that were not relevant to the rural setting in Shivgarh.
evidence: This explains the rationale for changing assessment tools.

claim: Air quality data were acquired using the Air Visual Node monitor (model B01MF6X1 YK, Atlanta Healthcare, Inc).
source: Air quality data were acquired using the Air Visual Node monitor (model B01MF6X1 YK, Atlanta Healthcare, Inc).
evidence: This describes the air quality monitoring equipment.

claim: The Air Visual Node device was selected based on validation data comparing it to a reference Beta Attenuation Monitor (BAM) in Beijing, China during June of 2015.
source: We selected this device based on validation data comparing the device to a reference Beta Attenuation Monitor (BAM) in Beijing, China during June of 2015 (Molenar, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Molenar, 2016.

claim: The task began with a 5-point calibration sequence.
source: The task began with a 5-point calibration sequence.
evidence: This describes the task procedure.

claim: The squares simultaneously appeared for 500ms and disappeared for 250ms during the 10 s trials.
source: The squares simultaneously appeared for 500ms and disappeared for 250ms during the 10 s trials.
evidence: This describes the timing of the visual stimuli.

claim: For the 'no-change' display, the colors of the squares remained constant throughout the trial.
source: For the 'no-change' display, the colors of the squares remained constant throughout the trial.
evidence: This describes the 'no-change' condition.

claim: For the 'change' display, one of the squares changed color after each disappearance.
source: For the 'change' display, one of the squares changed color after each disappearance.
evidence: This describes the 'change' condition.

claim: Memory load was varied between 1, 2, and 3 items on each side for 6- and 9-month-old infants.
source: Consistent with prior studies, memory load was varied between 1, 2, and 3 items on each side for 6- and 9-month-old infants and 2, 4, and 6 items on each side for 18- and 21-month-old infants.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation of memory load.

claim: Memory load was varied between 2, 4, and 6 items on each side for 18- and 21-month-old infants.
source: Consistent with prior studies, memory load was varied between 1, 2, and 3 items on each side for 6- and 9-month-old infants and 2, 4, and 6 items on each side for 18- and 21-month-old infants.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation of memory load.

claim: Infants were presented with 36 total trials in six blocks of six trials.
source: Infants were presented with 36 total trials in six blocks of six trials.
evidence: This describes the trial structure.

claim: Participants completed on average 20.99 trials in year 1 (SD = 9.72).
source: Participants completed on average 20.99 trials in year 1 (SD = 9.72) and 26.25 trials in year 2 (SD = 9.66).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data.

claim: Participants completed on average 26.25 trials in year 2 (SD = 9.66).
source: Participants completed on average 20.99 trials in year 1 (SD = 9.72) and 26.25 trials in year 2 (SD = 9.66).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the data.

claim: During each in-home assessment period, air quality data were collected across 3 days with the monitor placed at roughly head height in the room where the child typically slept or spent most of their time.
source: During each in-home assessment period, air quality data were collected across 3 days with the monitor placed at roughly head height in the room where the child typically slept or spent most of their time (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the air quality data collection procedure, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Air quality was monitored in 3-monthly intervals in-between the Year 1 and Year 2 laboratory visits for a maximum of 6 collection periods for each household.
source: Air quality was monitored in 3-monthly intervals in-between the Year 1 and Year 2 laboratory visits for a maximum of 6 collection periods for each household.
evidence: This describes the frequency of air quality monitoring.

claim: Data were collected from the AVN device every 10 s.
source: Data were collected from the AVN device every 10 s.
evidence: This describes the temporal resolution of air quality data collection.

claim: Households had to have at least 5 hr of recorded data in any given round for that round to be included in analysis.
source: Households had to have at least 5 hr of recorded data in any given round for that round to be included in analysis.
evidence: This describes a data quality criterion.

claim: After 8–10 months of use, a few of the air quality devices were returning very high or very low values.
source: After 8–10 months of use, a few of the devices were returning very high or very low values.
evidence: This describes a data quality issue.

claim: By the end of the 2-year study, 11 air quality devices had been retired.
source: By the end of the 2-year study, 11 devices had been retired.
evidence: This describes equipment attrition.

claim: Of the 9956 total trials used to calculate the scores, 3047 trials (30.6%) were manually coded.
source: Of the 9956 total trials used to calculate the scores, 3047 trials (30.6%) were manually coded.
evidence: This describes the proportion of manually coded data.

claim: 17% of the data were re-coded to check reliabilities.
source: We re-coded 17% of the data to check reliabilities.
evidence: This describes the reliability checking procedure.

claim: Reliabilities were very good with a mean Kappa for the 6-month cohort of 0.73 and a mean Kappa for the 9-month cohort of 0.83.
source: Reliabilities were very good with a mean Kappa for the 6-month cohort of 0.73 and a mean Kappa for the 9-month cohort of 0.83.
evidence: This is a reliability statistic from the data.

claim: Initial analyses revealed that the change preference measure was not robust longitudinally, that is, year 1 change preference scores did not predict year 2 change preference scores.
source: Initial analyses of these change preference scores revealed that the change preference measure was not robust longitudinally, that is, year 1 change preference scores did not predict year 2 change preference scores (note: a full correlation table for key measures used in the present study can be found in the supplementary materials; see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from preliminary data analysis.

claim: Sorting trials based on where infants are looking at the start of the first 'change' display yields two measures that are stable longitudinally – a 'first-look change' score and a 'first-look no-change' score.
source: Additional analyses from a forthcoming paper (Forbes et al., manuscript in preparation) revealed that sorting trials based on where infants are looking at the start of the first 'change' display (i.e. 1000ms) yields two measure that are stable longitudinally – a 'first-look change' score and a 'first-look no-change' score.
evidence: This is a finding from additional analyses, with reference to a manuscript in preparation.

claim: If infants start on the 'no-change' side, they should notice the 'sameness' if the number of items is within their visual working memory capacity and release fixation due to a lack of visual novelty.
